fact_en: Gliding means no wing-flapping at all — the animal just slowly drifts down as it moves through the air.
fact_bis: Ang pagdagan-dagan walay pagkampay sa pako — hinay-hinay ra monaog ang mananap samtang naglihok sa hangin.

findings.note: Gliding Uses No Wing Flaps. title_bis "Gliding nga Walay Pakpak" = "gliding WITHOUT WINGS" — `pakpak` is the noun wing throughout this corpus (64 cards), so the title asserts something false: gliders do have wings/membranes, they just do not flap. Body has it right ("walay pagkampay sa pako"), so this is title-only, but the false claim is the exact thing the card is correcting. (Body's `pagdagan-dagan` for gliding is systemic in the corpus — colugo/flying-fish cards — so I did not flag that.)

fact_en: A crab has ten legs in total — eight for walking and two that are pincer claws!
fact_bis: Ang alimango adunay napulo ka tiil — walo alang sa paglakaw ug duha nga sipit!

findings.note: Crab Legs. title_bis "Bitay sa Alimango" = "hanging of the crab"; `bitay` is hang/hanging in every other use in this corpus (98 bodies, and 5 other titles all about hanging roots/bats/objects), never leg — the word for legs here is `tiil`, which the body uses correctly ("napulo ka tiil"). Lower severity than the others because the body restores the fact; reported because it is a wrong noun in a title, the pattern the cat/`iro` case flagged.

title_bis: Dagkot nga Panit Batok sa Kalayo
fact_en: Some trees have thick bark that shields their living tissue inside, even during a forest fire.
fact_bis: Ang ubang kahoy adunay baga nga panit nga nagapanalipod sa buhi nga bahin niini, bisan adunay sunog sa lasang.

findings.note: Thick Bark Resists Fire. title_bis "Dagkot nga Panit Batok sa Kalayo" — `dagkot` in Cebuano is to LIGHT/kindle (a candle, a fire), not thick; on a fire card the title reads as "lit bark", the opposite of the card's point. Body restores it with `baga nga panit`. Same wrong title word in ffct-23565 ("Dagkot nga Bungbong" for Thick Walls), so it is a repeat defect worth grepping.

fact_en:
What happens in parasitism?

In parasitism, the parasite benefits while the host is harmed—like a tick sucking blood from a dog.
fact_bis:
Unsay mahitabo sa parasitism?

Sa parasitism, makiginabaw ang parasite samtang naano-ano ang host—sama sa garapata nga nangihap sa dugo sa iro.

findings.note: Parasitism. "sama sa garapata nga nangihap sa dugo sa iro" — `nangihap` = counting (ihap = to count), not sucking; corpus uses suyop/supsop/sipsip everywhere else and this is the only `nangihap` in 47k cards. The defining sentence is also carried by two non-words/unparseable forms — `makiginabaw` for "benefits" and `naano-ano` for "is harmed" — so the parasite-gains / host-is-harmed relationship plus its one concrete example are not recoverable from the Cebuano.

fact_en:
Is a snake's skin always cold and slimy?

Not true! Because a snake is cold-blooded, people assume its skin is always cold and slimy — but after basking, it's actually warm, dry, and smooth-scaled, not slimy at all.
fact_bis:
Kanunay ba bugnaw ug pisot ang panit sa bitin?

Dili tinuod! Tungod kay cold-blooded ang bitin, gituohan sa daghan nga kanunay bugnaw ug pisot ang panit niini — apan human magpa-adlaw, init gani kini, uga ug hamis nga himbis, dili pisot.

findings.note: Cold-Blooded Snakes. EN myth is "cold and slimy" skin; bis renders slimy as `pisot` in BOTH the question ("Kanunay ba bugnaw ug pisot ang panit sa bitin?") and the answer ("dili pisot"). `pisot` means uncircumcised (and is a kids' taunt word), not slimy — it is never corrected, so the myth the card exists to bust is not stated in Cebuano at all. Corpus evidence: `danlog` is the corpus's word for slippery/slimy (67 cards); this is the only `pisot` in 47k cards.

fact_en: When you visit a reef, the safest rule is: look, don't touch! Never grab or step on the fish or rocks.
fact_bis: Kung anaa sa bahura, ang pinakaluwas nga lagda mao: tan-awa lang, ayaw hikapa! Ayaw hikapa o tumbi ang isda o bato.

findings.note: title_bis 'Tan-aw dali Hikap Reef' for 'Look Don't Touch Reef' — the negation is gone and replaced by 'dali'. Corpus-wide check of every title containing 'dali' (60 cards) shows it always means fast/easy/quick, and as an imperative it means 'come/hurry', so the title reads 'Look, quickly touch the reef' — the opposite of the safety rule. Body ('tan-awa lang, ayaw hikapa') is correct, but this is a safety instruction inverted in the card's headline.

fact_en: Both armadillos and pangolins eat ants and termites — but the pangolin uses a long sticky tongue, while the armadillo digs with claws and eats with a regular mouth.
fact_bis: Pareho nga mokaon og hulmigas ug anay ang armadillo ug pangolin — pero mogamit ang pangolin og taas nga lapok nga dila, samtang maghukay ang armadillo gamit ang kuko ug mokaon gamit ang ordinaryong baba.

findings.note: Body: EN 'the pangolin uses a long sticky tongue' becomes 'mogamit ang pangolin og taas nga lapok nga dila' — lapok is MUD, not sticky (Cebuano for sticky is pilit/malagkit, which this corpus itself uses in ffct-36761 'malagkit'). Nothing in the card corrects it, so the Cebuano-only reader is told the pangolin has a long MUDDY tongue, and the mechanism that makes the tongue catch ants is gone.

fact_en:
Why is a rainforest floor so dark?

Because the thick canopy above blocks most sunlight! Less and less light reaches each layer as you go down.
fact_bis:
Ngano halos ngitngit ang salog sa rainforest?

Kay gisala sa baga nga canopy sa ibabaw ang kadaghanan sa kahayag! Mas mokunhod ang kahayag nga makaabot samtang mopaubos ka.

findings.note: title_bis 'Rainforest Salog Mabug-at' for 'Dark Rainforest Floor' — mabug-at is HEAVY, not dark (dark = ngitngit, which this card's own body uses). 35 corpus uses of mabug-at all mean heavy/weight, and the same swap recurs in ffct-23475 ('A Shadow, a Dark Area' -> 'Anino Mabug-at Lugar'), so the pair is a real corpus pattern, not a one-off typo.

fact_en: Animals survive hard seasons in three ways: sleeping (hibernation or estivation), traveling (migration), or changing and hiding.
fact_bis: Adunay tulo ka paagi ang mga mananap aron makalahutay sa lisod nga panahon: matulog, molalin, o mausab ug motago.

findings.note: title_bis 'Tulog Lubad o Kaupod' for 'Sleep, Migrate, or Adapt' — two of the three survival strategies are named as different things: 'lubad' is to fade/discolour (migrate = lalin, used correctly in the body as 'molalin') and 'kaupod' is a companion, not adapting/changing. Both words are hapax in the whole corpus, so this is a per-card corruption; the body lists the three strategies correctly.

fact_en: Detritivores like cockroaches and millipedes eat dead matter and shred it into tiny pieces so bacteria can decompose it faster.
fact_bis: Ang mga detritivore sama sa ipis ug ulahipan mokaon og patay nga butang ug gisi-gisonon kini sa gagmay nga tipik aron paspas nga mabungkag sa bakterya.

findings.note: EN lists detritivores as "cockroaches and millipedes"; bis renders millipede as "ulahipan", which is the centipede (a predator, not a detritivore). The card then teaches that ulahipan eat dead matter and shred it for bacteria — false for centipedes, and nothing in the card corrects the swap. Lower confidence than the first flag: Philippine usage does conflate centipede/millipede and there may be no common Cebuano term for millipede, so keeping the English word would have been the safe choice.

title_en: A Yawn Is a Deep Breath
fact_en: A yawn is a deep breath that fills your lungs with extra air!
fact_bis: Ang panghuyab usa ka lawom nga pagginhawa nga mopuno sa imong baga og dugang nga hangin!

findings.note: title_bis "Hiyaw nga Lawom nga Ginhawa" for "A Yawn Is a Deep Breath". Cebuano hiyaw = a shout/yell, not a yawn (yawn = huyab/panghuyab/hikab), so the title asserts "a shout is a deep breath" — a different bodily act. The body uses panghuyab correctly, so this is a title-only defect, but it is the same class as the cat-titled-iro case: the title names a different thing and is never corrected in the title itself.

title_bis: E. coli nga Mamumuo sa Biotech
fact_en: Tiny bacteria like E. coli are science's little workers — scientists grow them fast and reprogram them to make medicines, proteins, and enzymes!
fact_bis: Ang gagmayng bakterya sama sa E. coli morag gagmayng trabahante — dali silang paladakon sa mga syentista ug ma-engineer aron makahimo og gamot, protina, ug enzymes!

findings.note: EN: bacteria are reprogrammed "to make medicines, proteins, and enzymes". BIS: "ma-engineer aron makahimo og gamot, protina, ug enzymes". In Cebuano `gamot` means ROOT, not medicine (Cebuano for medicine is `tambal`) — this corpus itself uses `gamot` for plant roots ~520x (e.g. ffct-07243 stilt roots, ffct-07259 mangrove roots) and `tambal` for medicine ~330x. A child reading only the Cebuano gets "engineered to make roots, proteins and enzymes"; nothing in the card restores 'medicine'. Caveat: Tagalog-influenced (Davao) speakers may read `gamot` as medicine, so verdict is plausible rather than certain; title_bis of ffct-07258 in this same batch shows the same Tagalog-ism but its body carries the fact, so that one passes.
